subject: General
hook: The term report arrives this month. Read it in this order.
body: Most parents read top to bottom and land on the number. The useful information is somewhere else entirely.
slides: The term report lands this month.
Read it in this order, not top to bottom.
1. TEACHER COMMENTS FIRST. Specific comments mean they know your child. Generic ones mean they don't.
2. THE SPREAD, not the average. 80 in one subject and 45 in another is a different problem to 62 across the board.
3. CHANGE since last term. Direction matters more than position.
4. EFFORT vs ATTAINMENT. High effort, low attainment is a teaching problem. The reverse is a motivation one.
5. THE NUMBER. Last. It's a summary, not a diagnosis.
Then ask the school for the question-level breakdown. Most have it.
Comment EXAM for the questions to bring to the meeting.

subject: Mathematics
hook: 'She's fine, she just needs to practise more.' Ask which twenty minutes.
body:
Practice is not one thing. Twenty minutes on questions she can already do builds confidence and nothing else. Twenty minutes on the one topic she avoids is where the marks are.

Children, sensibly, choose the first. Nobody volunteers for the uncomfortable one.

So the question isn't whether she practises. It's whether anyone is choosing what she practises.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'She just needs to practise more. Okay — which twenty minutes?'
SPLIT (5-20s): 'Twenty minutes on what she can already do builds confidence and nothing else. Twenty on the topic she avoids is where the marks are.'
WHY (20-32s): 'Children choose the first. Every time. Nobody volunteers for the uncomfortable one.'
CLOSE (32-44s): 'The question isn't whether she practises. It's whether anyone is choosing what she practises.'

subject: General
hook: The December slump is real, and it isn't laziness.
body:
By week fourteen of a term, most children are running on empty. Attention drops, marks wobble, and the household reads it as attitude.

It's usually accumulated fatigue meeting the hardest content of the year, because syllabuses back-load the difficult chapters into the term nobody has energy left for.

The right response is triage, not pressure. Pick one subject. Leave the others to coast for three weeks.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'The December slump is real. It isn't laziness.'
BODY (5-20s): 'By week fourteen most children are running on empty. Attention drops, marks wobble, and everyone reads it as attitude.'
INSIGHT (20-36s): 'It's fatigue meeting the hardest content of the year — because syllabuses back-load the difficult chapters into the term nobody has energy left for.'
ADVICE (36-50s): 'Triage, not pressure. Pick ONE subject. Let the others coast for three weeks.'
CTA (50-54s): 'Send this to a tired parent.'

subject: Science
hook: Four sentences on a report card, and what each one actually means.
body: Report comments are written under time pressure, in a shared vocabulary. Once you know the code they're surprisingly direct.
slides: Four report card sentences. Decoded.
They're written fast, in a shared vocabulary. The code is readable.
'Could apply himself more' → usually one specific topic he's avoiding. Ask which.
'A pleasure to teach' → lovely, and tells you nothing academic. Ask a second question.
'Would benefit from consolidating basics' → there is a real gap below this year's work.
'Participates well in class' → check whether this survives written work. Often it doesn't.
None of these are criticisms of your child.
All four are invitations to ask one more question.

subject: English
hook: He can talk about the book brilliantly and writes half a page. That gap has a cause.
body:
Speaking is generative and forgiving — you can start a sentence without knowing where it ends. Writing is committed. Every sentence is permanent and judged.

Children who talk well and write badly are usually not short of ideas. They're short of a method for getting an idea out of their head and onto a page in a fixed order.

That method is teachable in about six weeks, and it's mostly planning, not vocabulary.

subject: Mathematics
hook: Two children, same 58. Completely different winters ahead.
body:
Child A got 58 by doing well on the first half of the paper and running out of time. Child B got 58 spread evenly, understanding roughly half of everything.

A has a pacing problem, fixable in about three weeks of timed papers. B has a comprehension problem, and that's a term.

The number is identical. The response should be nothing alike. This is why the mark, on its own, is nearly useless.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Two children. Both got 58. Completely different winters ahead.'
A (5-18s): 'Child A did well on the first half and ran out of time.'
B (18-30s): 'Child B scored evenly — understanding about half of everything.'
TURN (30-44s): 'A has a pacing problem. Three weeks of timed papers. B has a comprehension problem. That's a term.'
CLOSE (44-54s): 'Same number. Opposite response. Which is why the mark alone is nearly useless.'
CTA (54-58s): 'Comment MATHS for the diagnostic.'

subject: General
hook: Winter break: what actually helps, and what just ruins the holiday.
body: Three weeks off is long enough to lose fluency and short enough that cramming achieves nothing. There is a middle setting.
slides: Winter break. Three weeks.
Long enough to lose fluency. Too short for cramming to work.
DON'T: a full revision timetable. It won't survive week one, and failing it costs more than it gains.
DON'T: nothing at all. Arithmetic fluency and language recall genuinely decay.
DO: twenty minutes, four days a week, on ONE weak topic. That's it.
DO: read anything. Fiction counts. Comprehension is built by volume, not by worksheets.
DO: let them be bored. Boredom is where the recovery happens.
A rested child in January beats a resentful one who did more.

subject: General
hook: Comparing your child to their sibling is the most expensive sentence in the house.
body:
It never produces effort. It produces a story: I'm the one who isn't good at this.

Once a child holds that story, low marks stop being information and start being confirmation, and they'll protect the story by not trying — because not trying is a safer explanation for failing than trying and failing.

Compare a child to themselves last term. Nothing else.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'Comparing your child to their sibling is the most expensive sentence in the house.'
WHY (5-18s): 'It never produces effort. It produces a story: I'm the one who isn't good at this.'
MECHANISM (18-36s): 'Once that story exists, low marks stop being information and start being confirmation. And they'll protect it by not trying — because not trying is a safer explanation than trying and failing.'
FIX (36-48s): 'Compare a child to themselves last term. Nothing else.'

subject: Public Speaking
hook: Annual day is coming. The child with the small part is learning more than you think.
body:
Parents worry about the size of the role. Children mostly worry about whether they'll be embarrassed.

A three-line part, delivered without freezing, in front of four hundred people, does more for a child's willingness to speak in class in January than a lead role learned in panic.

Ask about the freezing, not the lines.

subject: Coding
hook: 'He's on the laptop all evening.' Ask what he's making.
body:
There is an enormous difference between consuming and building, and from the doorway they look identical.

A child watching gameplay and a child modding a game are in completely different developmental positions, and the second one is doing something closer to homework than you'd guess.

The question that separates them takes four seconds: show me what you made.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'He's on the laptop all evening. Okay — ask what he's MAKING.'
CONTRAST (5-20s): 'Consuming and building look identical from the doorway. A child watching gameplay and a child modding a game are in completely different places.'
POINT (20-34s): 'The second one is doing something much closer to homework than you'd guess.'
CLOSE (34-44s): 'The question that separates them takes four seconds. Show me what you made.'

subject: General
hook: What our mentors do in December that they don't do in August.
body:
August is diagnosis and gap-filling. December is protection.

By now a child has a term of accumulated fatigue, a report card they've read, and mocks in sight. Sessions get shorter and more targeted, we stop introducing new material three weeks before an exam, and we spend more time on what they already half-know.

Same mentor, different job. Teaching that ignores the calendar is teaching that ignores the child.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-5s): 'What our mentors do in December that they don't do in August.'
AUGUST (5-15s): 'August is diagnosis and gap-filling.'
DECEMBER (15-32s): 'December is protection. A term of fatigue, a report card they've read, mocks in sight. Sessions get shorter and more targeted.'
RULE (32-46s): 'We stop introducing new material three weeks before an exam. We work on what they already half-know.'
CLOSE (46-56s): 'Same mentor, different job. Teaching that ignores the calendar ignores the child.'

subject: General
hook: Five things our mentors are told never to say.
body: Every one of them is well-meant. Every one of them costs something.
slides: Five things our mentors are told never to say.
All well-meant. All expensive.
'It's easy.' — If they can't do it, you've just told them what that makes them.
'You should know this by now.' — Shame doesn't teach. It closes the session.
'Just remember it.' — If memory were the problem, they'd have done it.
'We're behind.' — Adds urgency to a child who already feels it. Manage the schedule quietly.
'Your brother found this fine.' — Never. Not once.
What they say instead: 'Show me what you tried.'

subject: General
hook: We ask every mentor to teach the same topic badly on purpose. Here's what it reveals.
body:
In the trial we give them a topic and a student who is quietly lost, and we watch what they do when the first explanation doesn't land.

Weak teachers say the same thing again, louder and slower. Good ones change the representation entirely — a diagram, an analogy, a smaller number.

The first explanation is easy. What you're hiring is the second and third.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-6s): 'We ask every mentor to teach a topic to someone who is quietly lost. Then we watch.'
TEST (6-20s): 'What matters isn't the first explanation. It's what they do when it doesn't land.'
WEAK (20-32s): 'Weak teachers repeat themselves. Louder. Slower.'
GOOD (32-46s): 'Good ones change the representation completely. A diagram. An analogy. A smaller number.'
CLOSE (46-56s): 'The first explanation is easy. What you're hiring is the second and the third.'

subject: General
hook: If your child likes their mentor but the marks haven't moved, say so.
body:
It's the hardest message for a parent to send, because the relationship is working and nobody wants to be the one who breaks it.

Send it anyway. Warmth without progress is a pleasant hour, and after two months it's an expensive one.

Usually it's a method problem, not a person problem, and it's fixable in a conversation. Occasionally it isn't, and then we change the mentor. Either way, week eight is the moment to raise it — not month five.

subject: General
hook: The note that goes home after a session your child found hard.
body: The easy weeks write themselves. This is the template for the difficult ones, because that note is where trust is either built or lost.
slides: The note after a session that went badly.
The easy weeks write themselves. This one matters more.
1. NAME IT PLAINLY. 'Today was hard. She got three of eight.'
2. SAY WHAT IT MEANS. 'That's the transposition gap, not the chapter.'
3. SAY WHAT'S NEXT. 'Two more sessions on this before we go back.'
4. SAY WHAT NOT TO DO. 'Please don't quiz her on it tonight.'
5. NO REASSURANCE PADDING. She'll be fine helps nobody.
A parent who gets this note stops guessing.
A parent who gets 'good session today!' starts.
